summary: Gives information on how to prepare RFCs and describes certain policies about their publication. It was the guide authors used for the format and process of the series. It replaced RFC 825, RFC 1111 and RFC 1543, and was in turn replaced by RFC 7322.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 2223 explains how to write a Request for Comments and how the series is published. It covers the format of the file, the sections every document must have, and the rules the RFC Editor follows when reviewing a submission.

subtitle: How to prepare a Request for Comments, and the rules for publishing one.

tldr.problem: The RFC series is made up of documents from many authors, and they have to be prepared in a way that works on any printer or screen and can be edited by the RFC Editor before publication.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2223 sets out the two allowed formats, ASCII and PostScript, with precise rules for page length, line length, fonts and headers. It also lists the sections every RFC must contain, and the policy the RFC Editor follows when reviewing a submission.
tldr.outcome: The document was the guide authors used for the format and process of the series until it was obsoleted by RFC 7322. It had earlier replaced RFC 825, RFC 1111 and RFC 1543, and was itself updated by RFC 5741 and RFC 6949.

today: RFC 2223 is an Informational document that has been obsoleted by RFC 7322, which carries the current instructions to RFC authors. It was also updated by RFC 5741 and RFC 6949. Before it was obsoleted, it replaced RFC 825, RFC 1111 and RFC 1543.

sections.title: What This RFC Covers
sections.content:
RFC 2223 tells authors how to prepare a Request for Comments and sets out the policies that govern how they are published. It was the guide in force when the RFC series was still produced as plain ASCII text files and the RFC Editor handled the editing by hand.

The series covers a wide range of interests. Its core topics are the Internet and the TCP/IP protocol suite, but any topic related to computer communication may be accepted at the discretion of the RFC Editor. Anyone may submit a memo. The largest source of memos is the IETF, whose working groups evolve their working memos, called Internet Drafts, until they feel they are ready, have them reviewed by the IESG, and then send them to the RFC Editor. Memos from independent sources are usually reviewed by the IESG as well, to see whether they relate to work in progress in the IETF working groups.

RFCs are distributed online as public access files, with a short message sent to the distribution list announcing that a memo is available. Because readers download the files and print or display them on their own equipment, the format has to work on a wide variety of printing and display equipment.

The primary version of an RFC was always an ASCII text file. Secondary versions in PostScript were allowed, to carry diagrams and drawings, and PostScript was chosen because printers that understand it were thought to be widely available. The RFC is candid about the drawback. Many readers work online with text tools such as emacs and grep, and excerpt RFCs in email, which is not practical with PostScript files.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC series takes submissions from anyone, and most of them come from the IETF working groups. Anyone may submit a memo. The Editor reviews each one and decides whether it becomes an RFC, and the Editor also checks that the document is in the house format before publication.

sections.title: Editorial Review and Publication
sections.content:
Documents proposed as RFCs are reviewed by the RFC Editor and possibly by other reviewers the Editor selects. The review may suggest improvements before publication. Sometimes the topic turns out to be the subject of an IETF working group, in which case the author can coordinate with the group, and the usual result is a revised Internet Draft that comes out of the IETF process as a recommendation from the IESG to the RFC Editor. Sometimes the submission is judged unsuitable for publication as an RFC.

The RFC Editor may make minor changes, especially to style and format and sometimes to the text, and may make more significant changes when the format rules are not followed. More often the memo goes back to the author for further work. Documents meant to become standards track RFCs must be approved by the IESG before they reach the Editor, and the communication runs from the Secretary of the IESG to the RFC Editor, usually citing the exact Internet Draft by file name. The Editor must assume that only that file is to be processed, so authors send small corrections separately rather than a new version of the document.

The time between submission and publication varies, because of the workload on the editorial staff. It is acceptable to query the Editor about the status of an RFC, but not more than once a week, and the two weeks before an IETF meeting are the busiest, so a memo submitted just before a meeting is likely to appear after it.

Contact details, distribution and the index come at the end of the RFC. Announcements go to two mailing lists, IETF-Announce and RFC-DIST, and a reader does not want to be on both. Several organisations maintain RFC index files, usually named rfc-index.txt, and copies taken from different sites may not be identical. The RFC itself raises no security issues.
sections.plainLanguage: A proposed RFC is reviewed by the RFC Editor, and anything meant to become an Internet standard is also reviewed and approved by the IETF's steering group. The Editor may tidy the formatting or send the document back for more work. The time from submission to publication varies, and it is fine to ask the Editor for a status once a week.

sections.title: Format Rules for ASCII and PostScript
sections.content:
The RFC allows two formats, ASCII and PostScript, and the Editor tries to keep a consistent style, which is easier if a submission already matches the style of the most recent RFCs. The author must submit an editable online document; the Editor may adjust the format or style and inserts the actual RFC number. Most RFCs are processed with the unix nroff program using the simple formatting commands from the ms macro package, and telling the Editor that a document was prepared with nroff helps.

The ASCII rules are precise. The character codes are ASCII. Each page is limited to 58 lines followed by a form feed on a line of its own. Each line is limited to 72 characters followed by carriage return and line feed. Overstriking and underlining are not allowed, and these limits cover any headers, footers, page numbers and left side indenting. Extra spaces must not be added to straighten the right margin, words must not be hyphenated at the right margin, and footnotes must not be used. A necessary note goes at the end of a section or of the document. Text within a paragraph is single spaced, with one blank line between paragraphs.

Because reformatting changes the page count and the page numbers where sections fall, cross references by section number are easier to keep consistent than cross references by page number.

The PostScript rules set the page size at 8 1/2 by 11 inches with a margin of 1 inch on all sides, main text of no less than 10 points with a line spacing of 12 points, and footnotes and graph notations of no smaller than 8 points with a line spacing of 9.6 points. Three fonts are acceptable, Helvetica, Times Roman and Courier, plus their bold-face and italic versions. Diagrams and images should be prepared on the lowest common denominator of PostScript, and a list of PostScript commands is not to be used.
sections.plainLanguage: An RFC is a plain text file. Each page holds at most 58 lines, each line at most 72 characters, and every page ends with a form feed. The alternative PostScript format has its own page size, margin, font and point size rules.

sections.title: Headers and Footers
sections.content:
There are three kinds of heading: the first page heading, the running header on later pages, and the running footer on every page.

The top of the first page carries, on the left, the traditional heading of the group that founded the RFC series, then the line Request for Comments with the number, which the Editor fills in at the last moment before publication, and then, if the RFC updates or obsoletes another, that indication on the third line. The category goes on the third or fourth line at the left and is one of Standards Track, Best Current Practice, Informational or Experimental. Other numbers in the series, such as the FYI, BCP and STD subseries, are also placed on the left. On the right, the author's name and organization occupy the first and second lines, and the month and year of publication the third. The title is centred below the rest of the heading, and periods or dots in titles are not allowed. When there are several authors from several organizations, the right side may carry extra lines to associate each author with the right organization.

The running header on page two and after has the RFC number on the left, the possibly shortened title centred, and the date on the right. The running footer on every page has the author's last name on the left, the category centred, and the page number on the right.
sections.plainLanguage: The first page carries the group name, the request for comments number, the author, the date and the category, with the title centred below. Later pages carry a running header with the RFC number and title, and a running footer with the author's name and the page number.

sections.title: The Sections Every RFC Must Have
sections.content:
Each RFC must carry a Status section on its first page with two elements: a paragraph describing the type of the RFC, and the distribution statement. The RFC gives the exact wording for the four categories. The Standards Track statement describes an Internet standards track protocol and points readers to the current edition of Internet Official Protocol Standards for the state and status of the protocol. Best Current Practice states that the document specifies an Internet Best Current Practice. Experimental says the memo defines an Experimental Protocol and does not specify an Internet standard of any kind. Informational says the memo provides information and does not specify an Internet standard of any kind. All four end with a statement that distribution of the memo is unlimited.

Immediately after the Status section comes the copyright notice, and the full copyright statement goes on the last page. Each RFC should have an Introduction section that explains the motivation and, where appropriate, the applicability of the protocol. Normally this is the abstract from the Internet Draft, but the RFC offers alternatives for a protocol, a discussion, an interest or a status report, and says they need not be followed word for word as long as the intent is clear.

Nearly all RFCs contain citations to other documents, listed in a References section near the end, following the style used in recent RFCs, and the STD number must be included for protocols that have one. All RFCs must contain a section near the end discussing the security considerations of the protocol or procedures that are the main topic. Each RFC must end with the author's address, giving the name and postal address, the telephone number, optionally a fax number, and the email address.
sections.plainLanguage: Every RFC must have a Status section on its first page with one of four approved wordings, a copyright notice, a section on security considerations, and the author's address at the end. Most also have an Introduction that says why the document exists, and a References section.

sections.title: Updates and Obsoletes
sections.content:
Sometimes an RFC adds information to a topic already covered by an earlier RFC, and sometimes it replaces one entirely. Two terms cover these cases, Updates and Obsoletes. The terms Supercedes and Replaces are no longer used.

Updates refers to a newer item that cannot be used on its own, so it supplements a previous document. It is something to be added to or inserted into the document that already exists, and it has limited usefulness independently, like an addendum or separate extra information.

Obsoletes refers to an earlier document that this one replaces. A document that obsoletes an earlier one can stand on its own. It may contain revised information, or the same information plus new information, however brief, and it can be used alone without reference to the older document. The RFC gives the Assigned Numbers RFCs as an example where Obsoletes is the right term, because the new document folds new information into the existing text and is more up to date.

In lists of RFCs and in the RFC index, but not on the RFCs themselves, two further terms point forward in time. Obsoleted-by refers to the newer documents that replace the older one. Updated-by refers to the newer sections that will be added to the existing, still used, document.
sections.plainLanguage: Two terms cover how an RFC relates to an earlier one. An update adds to an earlier document and is useless on its own. An obsoletes replaces an earlier document and can be read on its own.
